title: Cavity control of quantum phase transitions in a two-dimensional kondo lattice
authors: Jun Mochida, Atac Imamoglu, Yuto Ashida
abstract: Cavity quantum electrodynamics offers a route to control quantum phases by using vacuum fluctuations of confined electromagnetic fields. In particular, planar cavities based on polar van der Waals materials can generate strongly confined modes and are promising for controlling two-dimensional correlated materials. Recently, moiré materials have become central platforms for studying two-dimensional heavy-fermion systems and their quantum phase transitions. Kondo lattices provide a prototypical model for studying quantum phase boundaries, driven by competition between Kondo screening and the ordering of local magnetic moments. We show that a cavity-induced interaction can shift the quantum phase transitions between a heavy-fermion phase and an antiferromagnetic phase in a two-dimensional Kondo lattice through a momentum-dependent self-energy of the conduction bands. For the longitudinal projected field motivated by h-BN hyperbolic phonon polaritons, the self-energy favors Kondo hybridization and expands the heavy-fermion region. Transverse and circular in-plane model structures give distinct effects, with the transverse case relatively favoring the magnetically ordered phase and the circular case lying between the longitudinal and transverse cases. These results indicate that electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations can effectively modify the control parameters of strongly correlated two-dimensional Kondo materials.
summary: This theoretical paper demonstrates that vacuum fluctuations from planar optical cavities can act as a tunable control knob for quantum phase transitions in 2D Kondo lattices. By calculating the cavity-induced self-energy, the authors show that the specific geometry of the electromagnetic field dictates whether the system stabilizes a heavy-fermion state or an antiferromagnetic magnetic order.
main_problem: The study investigates how vacuum fluctuations from confined electromagnetic cavities can be used to actively control quantum phase transitions (QPTs) occurring in two-dimensional Kondo lattices.
main_result: Cavity-induced interactions modify the conduction band via a momentum-dependent self-energy, demonstrating that the geometry of the cavity field (longitudinal vs. transverse) dictates whether the system favors a heavy-fermion or magnetically ordered state.
method: The analysis employs mean-field theory applied to an effective periodic Anderson model coupled to cavity modes, calculating leading-order corrections via self-energy renormalization.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 2D Kondo lattice, modeled by coupling conduction electrons and localized f-moments. The Hamiltonian includes terms for the electronic structure, local moments, and the cavity field, which mediates an effective electron-electron interaction.
key_observables: Quantum phase transition boundaries (Heavy-fermion vs. Antiferromagnetic), Kondo hybridization order parameter ($P$), renormalized energy bands ($E_{\pm}^k$).
important_parameters: Cavity coupling strength ($\eta$), filling fraction ($ho_e$), and the geometry of the cavity field (longitudinal, transverse, circular).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a perturbative treatment for the cavity interaction ($\eta \ll 1$) and relies on mean-field approximations for both the Kondo screening and magnetic ordering.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the polarization dependence of the self-energy $\Sigma(k)$ in square lattices, phase diagrams showing transition boundaries vs. coupling strength ($\eta$), and shifts in the critical coupling constant ($J_K$).
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the coupled Hamiltonian to deriving an effective electron-electron interaction via virtual photon exchange. It then applies mean-field theory to compare the free energies of the heavy-fermion phase against magnetically ordered states, analyzing results for different lattice geometries.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges cavity QED (AMO physics) with strongly correlated matter by showing how external electromagnetic fields can tune fundamental many-body parameters like exchange couplings and hybridization strengths in solid-state systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Schematic setup of a two-dimensional Kondo lattice material coupled to a planar cavity mode. Con- duction electrons in the two-dimensional Kondo lattice layer couple to the cavity mode, while the localized mo- ments are treated as decoupled from the cavity field.

FIG. 2: The self-energy Σ(k) in momentum space for the triangular lattice at ρe = 0.7. The black dotted line shows the bare conduction-electron Fermi surface at this filling. The self-energy has a clear momentum de- pendence, and the pattern changes with the polarization structure. From top to bottom, these are the longitudinal structure and the transverse and circular model struc- tures, respectively.

FIG. 4: The mean-field parameters of ground states near the phase transition point at ρe = 0.7 and η = 0. The Kondo hybridization P is finite in the heavy-fermion phase, while the in-plane magnetic order parameter M∥ characterizes the 120-degree AFM phase.

FIG. 3: Energy crossing between the heavy-fermion phase and the 120-degree antiferromagnetic phase at ρe = 0.7 for the longitudinal structure. The upper and lower panels show η = 0 and η = 0.4, respectively. The two panels use the same horizontal range. The 120-degree AFM phase has the lower energy at smaller JK, while the heavy-fermion phase becomes lower at larger JK.

FIG. 5: JK–η phase diagram for the triangular lattice at ρe = 0.7. The phase diagram is obtained by solving the self-consistent equations for each phase and comparing the corresponding ground-state energies. The horizontal axis shows the Kondo coupling JK, and the vertical axis shows the cavity coupling strength η. The heavy-fermion region expands toward smaller JK for the longitudinal case, while the 120-degree AFM region expands for the transverse model case. The circular model case gives a transition line between these two cases.
